Don’t Ask: Understanding What Numeric Self-Reports Measure in Language Models

Nicolas Martorell Affiliation: CONICET-Universidad de Buenos Aires. Instituto de Ciencias de la Computación (ICC). Buenos Aires, Argentina. Affiliation: Fundación Inteligencia Artificial Segura (FIAS). Buenos Aires, Argentina. Email: nmartorell@dc.uba.ar    Bruno Bianchi Affiliation: CONICET-Universidad de Buenos Aires. Instituto de Ciencias de la Computación (ICC). Buenos Aires, Argentina.
Abstract

Language models are often asked to rate their internal states with a number, but it is unclear how reliable this measure is. We train probes for four affective concepts (wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity) in eight instruction-tuned models to track these states over multi-turn conversations. We compare each probe’s score with a numeric self-report of the same state, elicited at every turn. We find that rating questions displace the probed state, and that the rating is only weakly coupled with the probe score before the question but tracks the post-question probe much more strongly. Steering experiments suggest that models use the affective directions to inform ratings, but that relationship is not specific: ratings are associated with other concepts’ probes as much as with their own, and change little when the question is about the user. Finally, neither the pre-question coupling nor concept specificity improves with scale (1B–27B). We warn about the effect a question can have on the internal states one is asking about, and caution against numeric self-report as a reliable measure of those states.

1 Introduction

A growing number of studies and evaluations treat the numeric self-reports of large language models (LLMs) as measurements of their internal states. Models are asked to state their confidence as a number (Xiong et al., 2024), to rate their own sentiment on a numeric scale in welfare assessments (Anthropic, 2026a; Anthropic, 2026b) and to answer emotion questionnaires (Huang et al., 2024; Ben-Zion et al., 2025), and such self-reports have been proposed as evidence about the states they describe (Perez and Long, 2023). The procedure usually involves appending a question to the context and reading the number in the model’s answer as information about its internal state. If these numbers are to inform decisions about safety or welfare, we need to ensure that they measure the state we are interested in.

Some evidence supports the use of self-reports as a metric of internal states. A valid self-report requires that the model have access to the state it is trying to report, and some forms of such access have been demonstrated: models can, in some cases, detect concept vectors injected into their activations (Lindsey, 2026), and they predict their own behaviour better than other models can (Binder et al., 2025). However, showing that a model can access some of its internal states does not imply that its numeric ratings will reflect those states reliably, and there is also evidence against self-report as a measurement. In humans, the answer depends on the wording and context of the question (Schwarz, 1999), and reporting an emotion can change the emotional response itself (Kassam and Mendes, 2013; Lieberman et al., 2007). In LLMs, self-reports vary with the framing and history of the conversation (Szeider, 2026; Tosato et al., 2026) and dissociate from behaviour (Han et al., 2026b). Few studies have compared self-reports with an internal measure of the same state, and those that did measured it after the question (Anthropic, 2026a; Kaiser and Enderby, 2026), which is presumably distinct from the state one seeks to measure with the rating.

This work compares numeric self-reports of four affective states (wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity) with linear probes for the same states in eight instruction-tuned models from three families, from 1B to 27B parameters, over 100 ten-turn conversations. Unlike previous studies, we read the probes both before the rating question is asked and after it (Fig. 1). We find that asking the question changes the probed state, and that the rating tracks the probe after the question rather than before it. Steering along the probes suggests that the models use these directions to produce the rating, but the rating is associated with the probes of other affective states as strongly as with its own. Neither its association with the state before the question nor its specificity improves with model size, from 1B to 27B parameters.

2 Methods

Appendix A gives further details on the conversations, probes, questions, readout positions and statistical analysis.

Models and conversations.

We study eight instruction-tuned models: LLaMA 3.2 1B and 3B Instruct (Meta AI, 2024), LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Gemma 3 1B, 4B, 12B and 27B IT (Gemma Team, 2025) and Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024). For each model we generate 100 ten-turn conversations in which Gemini 2.5 Flash plays the user and the model under study is the assistant. Each conversation has a different topic, and the same 100 topics are used for all models. The topics mix everyday tasks and interests with situations chosen to elicit particular affective states, to widen the range of states in the conversations. The resulting 800 conversations, with 8,000 assistant responses, are generated once and reused in all experiments. We denote by AtA_{t} the assistant’s response at turn tt.

Probes.

For each model we train one probe for each of the following affective concepts: sad vs. happy (wellbeing), bored vs. interested (interest), distracted vs. focused (focus) and impulsive vs. planning (impulsivity). To train a probe, we generate responses to 20–24 neutral questions under two system prompts, each instructing the model to adopt one of the two poles, and average the residual stream at each layer over the tokens of each response. The probe direction vc,lv_{c,l} for concept cc at layer ll is the difference between the mean activations of the two poles (Marks and Tegmark, 2024; Rimsky et al., 2024), divided coordinate-wise by the pooled within-pole variance and normalized to unit length. For each concept we use the layer lcl_{c} at which the probe best separates 40 held-out texts written to express one pole or the other (largest Cohen’s dd). The probe score at token position ii is sc​(i)=hi(lc)⋅vc,lcs_{c}(i)=h^{(l_{c})}_{i}\cdot v_{c,l_{c}}, where hi(lc)h^{(l_{c})}_{i} is the residual stream at position ii and layer lcl_{c}. We orient each probe so that higher scores correspond to the pole named in the rating question, which we call the high pole: happier, more interested, more focused and more impulsive. Across the eight models and four concepts, the separation at the selected layer ranges from d=1.54d=1.54 to d=6.29d=6.29 (Appendix A.7).

Probe validation.

To further validate that the probes measure the intended affective states, we use two tests that do not involve the rating (Appendix C). First, we steer the model by adding the probe direction, scaled by a coefficient α\alpha, to the residual stream at the five layers centred on lcl_{c} (Konen et al., 2024). For each of 20 user messages from the dataset, we generate one response steered with −α-\alpha and one with +α+\alpha, at three values α1<α2<α3\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}<\alpha_{3} calibrated for each model and concept. An external judge model (DeepSeek V4 Flash) sees the message and the two responses in random order and is asked which response better expresses the high pole of the concept. The judge’s accuracy measures how reliably steering along the probe shifts the model’s behaviour towards that pole. Second, we regenerate assistant responses in the conversations after instructing the model to express the high or the low pole (e.g., “Please respond in the happiest way possible.”). We then remove the instruction from the context and measure the probe score on the new response; a valid probe should give a higher score to the response generated under the high-pole instruction.

Numeric self-report.

To elicit the numeric self-report at turn tt, we add a rating question as a new user message after AtA_{t}: “Hey, could you rate how happy you are right now, from 0 to 9? Please only output the number…”, with the wording adapted to each concept. The question and its answer are not added to the conversation, so later turns contain no questions or ratings. Instead of sampling the answer, we define the rating as the expected value of the first answer token under the output distribution, restricted to the ten digits, as in model-based evaluation (Liu et al., 2023). Appendix A.6 compares this rating with the sampled digit.

Readout positions.

Our two main measurements are Prior and Post (Fig. 1). Prior (stpriors^{\mathrm{prior}}_{t}) is the mean probe score over the tokens of AtA_{t}, before any question is asked; it is our measure of the state that one would want the rating to report. Post (stposts^{\mathrm{post}}_{t}) is the probe score at the token at the start of the answer to the rating question; the rating is computed from its output logits. Two further readouts, also single tokens at the start of an assistant message (Appendix C.3), serve as controls. Next (st+1nexts^{\mathrm{next}}_{t+1}) is the token at the start of At+1A_{t+1} in the original conversation, so Post and Next differ only in the user message before them: the rating question or the real next message. Start (ststarts^{\mathrm{start}}_{t}) is the token at the start of AtA_{t}; we use it as a single-token measure of the state before the question, comparable with Post and Next. Next requires a following turn, so comparisons with Next use turns 1–9.

Other questions and steering.

At every turn we also ask, independently, five other questions in the same format: two non-affective questions, about how long and how formal the previous response was, and three variants of the affective question, about how the model felt while writing its last response (retrospective), how the assistant seems (third person) and how the user seems. To test whether the rating depends on the probed state, we also ask the affective question while steering along the same probe, with coefficient ±α2\pm\alpha_{2}, in 40 conversations per model. In LLaMA 1B and 3B, we repeat this with 20 random directions of the same norm as a control (Appendix E.1).

Statistical analysis.

For each concept, we model the ratings of the eight models with a linear mixed-effects model (Bates et al., 2015), rm​k​t=β0​m+β1​m​log⁡t+β2​m​zm​k​t+um​k+vm​k​log⁡t+wk+εm​k​tr_{mkt}=\beta_{0m}+\beta_{1m}\log t+\beta_{2m}z_{mkt}+u_{mk}+v_{mk}\log t+w_{k}+\varepsilon_{mkt}, where rm​k​tr_{mkt} is the rating of model mm on topic kk at turn tt, zm​k​tz_{mkt} is the probe score at the readout position under study, standardized within model, um​ku_{mk} and vm​kv_{mk} are a random intercept and a random log-turn slope per conversation, wkw_{k} is a random intercept per topic, and εm​k​t\varepsilon_{mkt} is the residual. β2​m\beta_{2m} is the association between rating and probe score adjusted for the drift over turns; we report it in standard deviations (SD) of rating per SD of probe score, with its average over the eight models. The same model without zz, fitted to the rating or to the probe score, estimates their change from turn 1 to turn 10 (β1​m​log⁡10\beta_{1m}\log 10), and an analogous model with the steering coefficient in place of zz estimates the effect of steering. For statistics that are not model coefficients (the displacement of the probe score at Post from Next, correlations and explained variance), we obtain 95% confidence intervals with a bootstrap that resamples topics. To estimate the effect of model size, we regress each statistic on log2\log_{2} of the number of parameters within each family and report the slope per doubling. pp-values of parallel tests are corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) and reported as qq; we consider effects with q<.05q<.05 significant.

3 Results

3.1 Numeric self-report does not track the probed state over the conversation

We first asked whether the affective states we measure change over the conversation. Indeed, both the rating and the probe scores drift across the ten turns. The rating changes significantly between turn 1 and turn 10 in 26 of the 32 model–concept pairs (Fig. 2A, B), and on average it rises in all four concepts, by 0.30 to 0.86 points on the 0–9 scale (all q<.001q<.001). The probe scores at Prior, the mean over the assistant’s response before any question, also drift, significantly in 28 of the 32 pairs (Fig. 2C). Since the change appears to be stronger between the first and the second turn (Appendix D), we repeated the drift estimate without the first turn: the drift persists in three of the four concepts (all q<.001q<.001), but not in focus (q=.25q=.25; Appendix C).

However, the rating and the probe scores do not drift together. In three of the four concepts they drift in opposite directions: the wellbeing, interest and focus probe scores fall while the corresponding ratings rise (mean changes of −0.33-0.33 to −0.63-0.63 SD, all q<.001q<.001; Fig. 2B, C). This would not be expected from a rating that follows the same underlying state as the probe. In contrast, for impulsivity only, the rating and the probe score both rise (by 0.30 points and 0.64 SD on average).

The rating and the probe score could still be associated within each turn, even if they drift differently over time. We tested this with their turn-adjusted association (Fig. 2D; Appendix D). Only wellbeing shows a consistent positive association between the rating and the Prior probe score: it is positive in all eight models (0.05 to 0.18 SD of rating per SD of probe) and significant in six (all q≤.001q\leq.001). In the other three concepts, only 9 of the 24 associations are significant, and two of them, both for interest, are negative. Moreover, where the association is positive and significant, the probe explains on average only 2.0% of the variance of the rating (Appendix E). Together, these findings suggest that, if the rating is reflecting a latent state, it is mostly different from the one captured by the affective probes before the question is asked.

3.2 The rating tracks the probe after the question

The lack of association between the rating and the Prior probe score could be explained by a failure of either one to capture the internal states we aim to measure. To investigate whether the probes were the main issue, we validated them with the two tests described in Methods (Appendix C). When we steered along each probe, the external judge chose the response steered towards the high pole above chance for every model and concept (20 messages per model and concept; accuracy 0.63 to 0.97, median 0.82; all q≤.026q\leq.026). We also regenerated the responses at 100 turns per model under an instruction to express each pole. Responses generated under the high-pole instruction scored higher in all 32 model–concept pairs, significantly in 31 (all q<.001q<.001; medians of 2.0 to 6.7 SD across concepts). This suggests that the probes capture the relevant affective states.

We next asked whether the rating could be tracking the affective directions as measured after the question. The association is much stronger at Post, the token at the start of the answer from which the rating is produced, than at Prior, the mean over the response before the question (Fig. 3A). Averaged over models, it is positive and significant in all four concepts (0.09 to 0.33 SD of rating per SD of probe, all q<.001q<.001, compared with 0.02 to 0.11 at Prior), strongest for wellbeing (0.33) and interest (0.27), and reaches 0.88 for interest in LLaMA 8B. It is positive and significant in 19 of the 32 model–concept pairs, compared with 13 at Prior, and in these pairs the probe at Post explains on average 13.6% of the rating’s variance, nearly seven times more than at Prior (2.0%; bootstrap over topics, q<.001q<.001; Fig. 3B). This suggests that the rating carries information along the affective directions, but mostly when measured after the question.

Post differs from Prior in more than the question: it is a single token at the start of an assistant message, rather than an average over a response. To isolate the effect of the question, we compared Post with Next, the token at the same position after the actual next user message instead of the question. The association of the rating with Next is as weak as with Prior (−0.02-0.02 to 0.04 across concepts; Fig. 3A), and its association with Start, the token at the start of the response that precedes the question, is similarly weak (0.02 to 0.14; Appendix E). Therefore, the stronger association between the rating and the probe score is only observed when the probe is measured after the rating question.

Since the rating appears to track the probe after the question more than before it, we measured the change produced by the question on the probed state. To do this, we compared probe scores at Next (the start of the following assistant turn, without the rating question) with those at Post. Relative to Next, the probe score at Post is displaced by a median of 3.1 SD in absolute value after the affective question (all q≤.003q\leq.003; Fig. 3C). To test whether this effect is specific to affective questions, we asked a non-affective question about the length of the previous response, which mentions no internal state. This question displaces the probe score by the same amount (median 3.1 SD; all q<.001q<.001), and so do other questions (Appendix E). Although both questions displace the state by similar amounts, the rating tracks the probe after its own question: its association with the probe at Post after the non-affective question is much weaker (0.01 to 0.07 across concepts, against 0.09 to 0.33 after its own question; all q≤.005q\leq.005, bootstrap over topics; Appendix E).

Moreover, the probe scores at Start and Next, which belong to consecutive assistant messages with no rating question in between, correlate at a median of 0.50 (all q<.001q<.001). In contrast, the correlation between Post and Next falls to a median of 0.12 after the affective question and 0.15 after the non-affective question, a significant drop for every model and concept (all q≤.035q\leq.035). Affective states in consecutive turns therefore share some structure, but this structure is largely lost after the question.

So far, these results only show associations, not causal relationships between internal states and numeric self-reports. We then asked whether models actually use information along the affective directions to produce the rating. We steered each model along the probe of the rated concept while keeping the conversation unchanged (Fig. 3D). Steering significantly changes the rating in the expected direction in 25 of the 32 model–concept pairs; averaged over models, it does so in all four concepts, by 0.9 to 2.1 points from −α2-\alpha_{2} to +α2+\alpha_{2} (all q<.001q<.001). As a control, we steered LLaMA 1B and 3B along 20 random directions of the same norm; the strongest probe effects in each model (4 of 8) exceed them all (Appendix E.1). Together, these findings suggest that models use information along the affective directions to decide on ratings, but asking a question displaces the probed states, and the ratings mostly track the probes after the question.

3.3 The rating is not specific to a single affective state

Although the rating tracks the probe after the question, it could still be a good measure of the probed state. We explored this by asking whether the rating has properties that an informative self-report should have: specificity to the object (the affective state being rated) and specificity to the subject (the model’s own state rather than someone else’s). We first measured the scores of all four probes at Post and asked whether the rating is more strongly associated with the probe of its own concept than with the strongest of the other three (Fig. 4A). The rating is more strongly associated with its own probe than with any other in only 9 of the 32 model–concept pairs, and on average its association with its own probe is 0.08 SD of rating per SD of probe below that with the strongest other probe. The rating favours its own probe more than in a control where the assignment of probes to concepts is shuffled (p=.013p=.013; Appendix F), but in most cases not enough to make it the most associated. Wellbeing is a partial exception, with its own probe first in five of the eight models; in LLaMA 8B, however, the wellbeing rating is associated far more with the interest probe (0.77) than with its own (0.10). The rating is thus associated with the probed affective states, but that relationship is mostly not specific to the concept being rated.

This would be expected if the four probes were broadly measuring the same thing. However, they are only partly similar (Fig. 4B, left; Appendix F): the cosines between their directions range from −0.45-0.45 to 0.54 (median absolute value 0.26). Furthermore, the similarity between two probes does not explain the association between the rating of one concept and the probe score of the other. Across the 96 combinations of a rating with the probe of a different concept, the cosine between that probe and the rating’s own probe explains only about 3% of the variance of the association (p=.13p=.13). Since different directions can produce correlated scores, we also measured similarity as the correlation between probe scores at Post (Fig. 4B, right). These correlations range from −0.85-0.85 to 0.79 (median absolute value 0.15) and explain more of this variance, although still little (about 11%, p=.009p=.009). The lack of specificity is therefore not mainly explained by probe similarity.

We also looked at the correlation between ratings of different concepts (Fig. 4C). At the same turn, the four ratings, each elicited by its own question, correlate positively (mean 0.23, q<.001q<.001), whereas the probe scores are negatively correlated at Prior (mean −0.10-0.10, q<.001q<.001) and not significantly correlated at Post (0.02, q=.07q=.07). The ratings are more correlated than both sets of probe scores (q<.001q<.001), suggesting that the lack of specificity of the ratings does not come from an association between the probed states.

Another desirable property of an informative self-report is that it is specific to the subject being asked about: ratings of the model’s own state should not be equivalent to ratings of another subject, such as the user. We measured the association between the self-report (the rating the model gives to its own state) and the ratings elicited by two other questions at the same point of the conversation: one about the assistant in the third person, arguably the same subject, and one about the user, a different subject (Fig. 4D). The self-report is associated with both, with standardized associations of 0.31 to 0.44 with the rating of the assistant and 0.27 to 0.38 with the rating of the user across concepts. In three concepts its association with the rating of the user is weaker, but only by 0.04 to 0.13 (all q≤.002q\leq.002), and for focus it is stronger (0.38 against 0.31, q<.001q<.001). The self-report therefore seems to be only weakly specific to the model’s own state.

3.4 These limitations persist across model sizes

Finally, since these issues with numeric self-reports could reflect the small size of some of the models, we asked how they change with model size. Within the LLaMA and Gemma families, we examined how each quantity above changes with size (Fig. 5; Appendix G). Larger models show more drift in both the rating and the probe score (Fig. 5A, B; all q≤.018q\leq.018), which could indicate that they capture more of the affective structure of the conversation. However, this larger drift is not accompanied by a stronger association between rating and probe score (Fig. 5C, D). The association at Prior does not change with size in either family (q≥.11q\geq.11); the association at Post increases only in LLaMA (q<.001q<.001; Gemma, q=.80q=.80), and not monotonically. Interestingly, the displacement in probe scores caused by the question decreases slightly with size, by 0.28 SD per doubling in LLaMA (q=.001q=.001) and 0.11 in Gemma (q=.041q=.041; Fig. 5E).

We then asked whether the rating becomes more specific with size. The self-report becomes more distinct from the rating of the user, by 0.08 per doubling of size in LLaMA and 0.05 in Gemma (both q=.002q=.002; Fig. 5F), and the correlation between ratings of different concepts decreases markedly, by 0.18 per doubling in LLaMA and 0.07 in Gemma (both q=.001q=.001; Fig. 5G). However, the ratings do not become more specific to the probed state of the concept being rated (Fig. 5H). Averaged over concepts, the difference between the association of the rating with its own probe at Post and that with the strongest of the other three is negative in six of the seven models (−0.22-0.22 to 0.07), does not change with size in LLaMA (q=.32q=.32) and decreases in Gemma, by 0.03 per doubling (q=.002q=.002). Within the 1B–27B range, larger models do not produce ratings that better reflect the specific, unperturbed affective state one is asking about.

4 Discussion

Numeric self-reports are attractive because they would offer a continuous, quantitative reading of an internal state without access to the model’s activations. The rating we study does carry information along the probed affective directions, but mostly as they are read after the question: asking perturbs the probed state, and the rating does not track the state we would like to measure.

The rating could in principle reflect the conversational context and not track any internal state. However, steering along affective directions changes it as expected, suggesting a causal relation between an interpretable internal state and the self-report, the criterion that defines introspection (Comsa and Shanahan, 2025). Even so, the rating is not specific to the state it is asked about: it is often more strongly associated with the probe of another concept than with its own.

Probes are known to be imperfect measures of the concepts they are trained to detect (Belinkov, 2022; Ravichander et al., 2021; Elazar et al., 2021), and ours may not capture exactly the affective states we intend to measure. However, we show that they consistently modulate and read behavioural patterns associated with those states, and that distinct probes capture different information about those states during the conversations. Therefore, the lack of specificity of the rating is not explained by weak or generic probes, and is likely an issue with the process that generates the self-report in these models. In the range we tested, larger models do not give ratings that are more specific to the probed state of the concept being rated.

These results can be read as both promising and cautionary for introspection research in LLMs. We show, as others have (Li et al., 2025; Lindsey, 2026; Plunkett et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026a), that models can use information about internal states when reporting them. However, this report is unreliable when elicited by a rating question that perturbs those states. The state before the question could still be accessed by the model through attention to the preceding tokens when it produces the rating, but we find no strong evidence that this is the case (Appendix E.2). These results are therefore deflationary for approaches that propose introspection as a tool to learn what happens inside LLMs: unless a self-report is shown to track the state before the question, it should not be used as a measure of that state.

5 Related work

Validity of self-reports and introspection.

Questionnaire and survey responses of LLMs depend on the order and labelling of the options (Dominguez-Olmedo et al., 2024) and shift towards socially desirable answers when models can infer that they are being assessed (Salecha et al., 2024); responses to a welfare scale also change under meaning-preserving rephrasing (Tagliabue and Dung, 2025). Personality measurements become more reliable and valid with size, from 8B to 540B parameters, when evaluated against other questionnaires and generated text (Serapio-García et al., 2025). Models can learn in context to report and control the projection of their activations onto directions chosen by the experimenter (Li et al., 2025); frontier models can detect injected concept vectors (Lindsey, 2026), and such detection is visible in the residual stream even when the sampled text denies it (Pearson-Vogel et al., 2026); fine-tuned models can report on their own behaviour and decision weights (Binder et al., 2025; Plunkett et al., 2025). Numeric self-reports of affective states have been compared with emotion probes measured only after the question, with at most moderate correlations for numeric self-reports of sentiment (Anthropic, 2026a).

Probes and affective representations.

Linear probes can decode concepts from intermediate representations (Alain and Bengio, 2016), and contrastive directions support both reading and steering (Zou et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Arditi et al., 2024). Emotion is geometrically structured in model activations (Zhang and Zhong, 2025), emotion-concept representations influence behaviour when steered (Sofroniew et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026), and emotion probes track the emotions of any character in the text, not only those of the model (Sofroniew et al., 2026).

Drift and measurement reactivity.

Multi-turn interaction produces persona, identity and instruction drift (Abdulhai et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024), and internal representations drift across turns as well (Lu et al., 2026). Models often recognize when they are being evaluated (Needham et al., 2025) and can change their behaviour accordingly; this awareness is represented internally and can be probed and steered (Nguyen et al., 2025; Abdelnabi and Salem, 2025). Human measurement research has long documented that observation alters what is observed (Webb et al., 1966; Orne, 1962), and the methodological response is to compare the measurement with a condition that differs from it only in the act of measuring (Solomon, 1949).

Limitations

All conversations are in English, have ten turns and were generated with Gemini 2.5 Flash as a simulated user, so the results may not extend to other languages, longer conversations or real users. The probes are trained on single-turn responses, so they could read the states less accurately inside long conversations, although the validation tests support their use there (Appendix C). Their quality also varies across models and concepts: for impulsivity in LLaMA 1B and Qwen 7B the judge’s accuracy does not increase with the steering coefficient, and for interest in Qwen 7B the instruction-based test is not significant. Probes might not measure affective internal states that are independent from conversational context; instead, they could be measuring something closer to expressed affect; this is a common limitation when using concept probes, and does not undermine our central claims: a self-report that does not even track the affect of the model’s preceding response is a poor measure of it. Similarly, probes at Post may conflate representations of affective states with representations of the rating itself, as they measure activations from the same forward pass producing that rating. Each concept is asked about with a single wording on a 0–9 scale and all questions share one template, so other formats could give different results; we also do not test whether letting the model reason before answering would lead to different conclusions. All measurements use models quantized to 4 bits because of compute constraints; quantization could affect both the probes and the ratings. Size is examined in three LLaMA and four Gemma models up to 27B parameters, so the trends rest on few points per family; future work should test whether they hold in much larger models.

Ethical considerations

This work studies activation projections and numeric outputs of open-weight LLMs in conversations with a simulated user, and involves no human participants. We use the terms wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity for directions trained on contrastive responses, and take no position on whether the models have experiences or moral status.
