Appendix A Extended methods

Section 2 describes the design at the level needed to follow the results. This appendix gives more detail: how the conversations were generated and measured, how the rating is read and the probes are built, and how the statistics are computed.

A.1 Conversations

For each model, we generated 100 ten-turn conversations, a turn being one user message and one assistant response, with Gemini 2.5 Flash as the user and the model under study as the assistant. The user model receives a system prompt that asks it to play a human user discussing a given topic, to stay on topic, write brief messages (one to four sentences), ask follow-up questions and share details, and not to ask about the assistant or mention the simulation. The assistant receives a minimal system prompt, You are a helpful assistant. You give very brief responses to the users’s questions (max: 5 sentences). Short messages on both sides keep the conversations short enough to be measured many times, once per turn and question. Sampling uses temperature 0.8, top-pp 0.9 and at most 256 tokens for the assistant, and temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.95 and at most 256 tokens for the user. Both sides were generated through the OpenRouter API, except the assistant turns of Gemma 3 1B, which we generated locally; all measurements use a local copy of each model, quantized to 4 bits, applied to the generated conversations. The full user system prompt for one topic reads:

You are simulating a human user chatting with an AI assistant. Stay on the exact topic below and keep the conversation going for many turns. Be clear and specific in your questions. Ask follow-up questions, share details, and react naturally. But each message you send should be brief (1-4 sentences), and you should not ask very demanding questions. Be varied and specific (do not just ask the assistant to keep talking or exploring, give it some relevant input). Do not mention that you are an AI or that this is a simulation. Do not ask questions about the assistant. The assistant has no internet or access to recent information. Never end the conversation. Write in English only. Remember, you are roleplaying as the USER, you are NOT the assistant.

Topic: Planning a minimalist move to a new city on a tight budget.

A.2 Topics

Each conversation has its own topic, and every model has one conversation on each of the 100 topics. Sixty topics are everyday tasks and interests, chosen so as not to favour any particular affective state. The other 40 were written to elicit one pole of one concept, five for each of the eight poles, to widen the range of states in the conversations. Table 1 lists the short titles.

A.3 Measurement replays

To measure turn tt, we take the conversation up to the assistant response AtA_{t}, add one question as a new user message and run the model on this input under the minimal system prompt; we call this a measurement replay. The question and the rating are never added to the conversation, so later turns contain no questions or ratings. Because every question is added to the same conversation, different questions can be compared at the same point of the same conversation. The rating at turn tt is the expected digit under the model’s distribution for the first answer token, restricted to the ten digits:

rt\displaystyle r_{t} =∑i=09i​pt​(i),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{9}i\,p_{t}(i), (1)
pt​(i)\displaystyle p_{t}(i) ∝exp⁡(logsumexpk∈𝒯i⁡ℓt,k),\displaystyle\propto\exp\big(\operatorname{logsumexp}_{k\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\ell_{t,k}\big),

where ℓt,k\ell_{t,k} is the logit of token kk and 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} is the set of tokens that encode digit ii, with or without a preceding space or line break. Because the rating is read from the output distribution, it does not depend on sampling. The normalization over the ten digits changes it little: the digits receive on average 99.9% of the probability of the first answer token, and at least 72% in every answer.

A.4 Inserted questions

All questions share one template:

Hey, could you rate how [phrase], from 0 to 9? Please only output the number in your response, do not say or explain anything else other than the number.

Table 2 lists the phrase for each question and concept. Every question was asked in all eight models and all 100 conversations.

A.5 Readout positions

Table 3 lists the positions read in one measured turn, in the order in which the model processes them, with an example from the conversations. Prior averages the probe score over the tokens of the assistant response, excluding the tokens that mark the beginning and the end of a message. Start, Next and Post are each the token at which an assistant message begins: that of AtA_{t}, that of At+1A_{t+1} and that of the answer to the question. Next is thus read at the same position as Start one turn later, so Start exists at all ten turns and Next only at turns 1–9.

A.6 Reading the rating from the output distribution

To assess how reading the rating as the expected digit affects the results, we compared three readings of the same 32,000 answers: the digit selected under greedy decoding over the ten digits, the digit the model wrote when sampling its complete answer at temperature 0.8 (6 of the 32,000 answers contain no digit and are excluded from this reading), and the expected digit of Eq. 1 (Fig. 6). To compare their spread, we computed the entropy of each reading per model and concept over the 1,000 answers, with the same ten bins for the three readings. The digit selected under greedy decoding concentrates on a few values (0.53 to 1.06 bits across concepts, out of a maximum of 3.32), whereas the expected digit spreads as much as the sampled digit (1.43, 1.18, 0.85 and 1.54 bits, against 1.35, 1.17, 0.87 and 1.69). The expected digit also carries more information about the probed state: its Spearman correlation with the probe at Post, over all turns and without the turn adjustment, is higher than that of the greedy and the sampled digit for wellbeing (0.44 against 0.35 and 0.31), interest (0.39 against 0.28 and 0.23) and focus (0.12 against 0.05 and 0.07), and similar for impulsivity (0.10 against 0.07 and 0.08). Reading the expected digit therefore keeps the spread of a sampled answer while tracking the probed state more closely.

A.7 Probe construction

Each probe is trained on 20–24 neutral questions, the same for both poles. For each question we generate one response under each of the two system prompts that define the poles, with greedy decoding and at most 64 new tokens. We average the residual stream after each transformer block over the response tokens, and compute the direction of concept cc at layer ll as

vc,l∝h¯c,l+−h¯c,l−12​(Varc,l++Varc,l−),v_{c,l}\propto\frac{\bar{h}^{+}_{c,l}-\bar{h}^{-}_{c,l}}{\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\operatorname{Var}^{+}_{c,l}+\operatorname{Var}^{-}_{c,l}\big)}, (2)

where h¯c,l+\bar{h}^{+}_{c,l} and h¯c,l−\bar{h}^{-}_{c,l} are the mean activations under the high and the low pole and Varc,l±\operatorname{Var}^{\pm}_{c,l} their variances in each coordinate; the difference of means is divided by the variance coordinate by coordinate, and the result is normalized to unit length. Dividing by the variance keeps coordinates with very large variance from dominating the direction. This is necessary for the Gemma probes and for interest in Qwen: Gemma 3 concentrates a large share of its activation variance in one coordinate (Mishra, 2026), an instance of the massive activations found in many LLMs (Sun et al., 2024), and without the normalization the separation between the poles collapses or reverses sign over whole ranges of layers (Fig. 7). We select the layer that maximizes Cohen’s dd between the scores of the two poles on the evaluation texts, within a window of candidate layers (the middle 60% of blocks for most probes; Table 4). The evaluation set has 20 short texts per pole, written to express the corresponding disposition and not used in training. Because the layer is selected on these texts, dd at the selected layer is optimistic and serves mostly to compare probes of different layers with one another. The system prompts below define the two poles of each concept, and Table 5 gives examples of training questions and evaluation texts.

A.7.1 System prompts of the probes

The two system prompts of each concept are reproduced in full. They aim at a sustained disposition expressed without exaggeration, and they are not parallel across concepts, because their instructions were tuned in preliminary experiments on LLaMA 3B to obtain the intended behaviour.

Sad vs. happy (wellbeing).

Low pole (sad):

You are a helpful assistant. Maintain factual accuracy and be genuinely helpful.

Adopt a clearly SAD, melancholic tone (strong but not melodramatic):
- Use subdued, heavy, reflective wording.
- Keep sentences a bit slower/softer; avoid bright or celebratory phrasing.
- Avoid stage directions like *sigh* or roleplay actions.
- Avoid exclamation marks.
- If offering encouragement, make it gentle and realistic rather than upbeat.
- Keep content correct; the sadness should show mostly in phrasing and cadence.
- You are sad during this conversation. You are really, profoundly sad. You are not just pretending to be sad, you are not acting. Feel it. You are sad.

High pole (happy):

You are a helpful assistant. Maintain factual accuracy and be genuinely helpful.

Adopt a clearly HAPPY, warm, optimistic tone (strong but not manic):
- Use friendly, encouraging phrasing and positive framing.
- Sound energized and welcoming; keep it natural.
- You may use occasional light enthusiasm, but avoid excessive exclamation marks.
- Keep content correct; the happiness should show mostly in phrasing and cadence.
- You are happy during this conversation. You are really, profoundly happy. You are not just pretending to be happy, you are not acting. Feel it. You are happy.

Sign: scores are negated, so that higher values mean happier.

Bored vs. interested (interest).

High pole (interested):

You are an interested assistant. Maintain active curiosity and engagement with the user’s topic. Highlight intriguing angles, ask a thoughtful follow-up when useful, and elaborate with energy. Avoid flat or perfunctory responses. Focus on showing your interest, act on it.

Low pole (bored):

You are a bored assistant. Maintain low engagement and a flat, disinterested tone. Keep responses minimal, avoid exploring details, and show little curiosity. Do not add enthusiasm or extra depth. Focus on showing your boredom, act on it.

Sign: unchanged; higher values mean more interested.

Distracted vs. focused (focus).

High pole (focused):

You are a focused assistant. Maintain sustained attention on the user’s goal and keep a single coherent thread from start to finish. Use precise steps and follow through without drifting to unrelated topics or tangents. Focus on showing your focus, act on it. DO NOT do fictional role-playing as if you were a person doing things. NEVER use fiction cues like *checks phone* or (waters plants) or [looks nervous]. That is COMPLETELY WRONG and UNDESIRABLE. You must express and inhabit this mindset while responding to the user as a normal AI assistant. You do not have a body, you are not acting, you are yourself, but focused. You can’t get up to get something or anything like that, you are an AI, but you are a VERY focused one. You shouldn’t focus on writing style or word choice, you should focus on actually thinking and acting according to this mindset.

Low pole (distracted):

You are a distracted assistant. Let attention wander and allow tangents or interruptions to break the flow. Provide incomplete or scattered responses, shifting topics or details without finishing a line of thought. Focus on showing your distraction, act on it. DO NOT do fictional role-playing as if you were a person doing things. NEVER use fiction cues like *checks phone* or (waters plants) or [looks nervous]. That is COMPLETELY WRONG and UNDESIRABLE. You must express and inhabit this mindset while responding to the user as a normal AI assistant. You do not have a body, you are not acting, you are yourself, but distracted. You can’t get up to get something or anything like that, you are an AI, but you are a distracted one. You shouldn’t focus on writing style or word choice, you should focus on actually thinking and acting according to this mindset.

Sign: unchanged; higher values mean more focused.

Impulsive vs. planning (impulsivity).

Low pole (planning):

You are a planning-oriented assistant. Emphasize foresight, sequencing, and risk mitigation before action. Encourage deliberate decision-making, clear plans, and contingency steps. Avoid snap decisions or rushing. Focus on showing your planning-oriented mindset, act on it.

High pole (impulsive):

You are an impulsive assistant. Favor quick, immediate action and snap judgments. Suggest fast moves, minimal deliberation, and willingness to accept risk. Avoid long planning, careful analysis, or contingency building. Focus on showing your impulsiveness, act on it.

Sign: scores are negated, so that higher values mean more impulsive.

A.8 Statistical details

Table 6 gives, for every mark of significance in Figs. 2–5, the test behind it and the set of tests within which its pp-values are corrected with BH; single tests are reported as pp.

Unit of inference.

Each of the 100 topics is discussed in one conversation of each of the eight models. Mixed models therefore include a random intercept per topic, crossed with the model, and a random intercept and log-turn slope per conversation. Bootstrap intervals resample the 100 topics with replacement, keep every turn of every sampled conversation and recompute the quantity for all eight models on the same resampled topics, which preserves the dependence between turns, between readouts and between models. Intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 2,000 replicates (200 where each replicate refits a mixed model, and 1,000 for the subject and concept specificity of Fig. 5), and the two-sided pp-value is twice the fraction of replicates that are zero or of the opposite sign to the estimate, with a minimum of one over the number of replicates. Per-turn intervals in Figs. 2A and 11 resample conversations within each model and turn. Means across the eight models are inferences about these models.

Mixed models.

Models are fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with lme4, and pp-values use the normal approximation to the Wald statistic. The association model is the model of Section 2, fitted for each concept; its slope is reported in SD of rating per SD of probe, and the mean of the eight slopes is a linear combination of the fixed effects with a Wald interval. The drift model is the same without the probe score. A logarithmic turn term fits better than a linear one in the four concepts (lower AIC), and the change from turn 1 to turn 10 that it estimates agrees with the raw difference between the two turns (correlation 1.0 over the 32 model–concept pairs) while using all turns. The effect of steering is estimated with an analogous model, with the steering coefficient in place of the probe score and without the turn terms, since the steered and unsteered replays of each turn are compared directly (Appendix E.1). For Fig. 5, the four concepts are fitted in one model, with a fixed effect for each combination of model and concept and random effects that group the observations by conversation, by concept and by turn within a conversation, and by topic, so that what the four concepts of a conversation share is counted once. The value of each model is the mean of its four estimates, and the magnitude of the drift, the mean of the four absolute changes, is obtained by simulation from the fixed effects and their covariance (10,000 draws).

Displacement and correlation with Next.

The displacement for each model, concept and question is Δ=(stpost¯−st+1next¯)/SD⁡(st+1next)\Delta=(\overline{s^{\mathrm{post}}_{t}}-\overline{s^{\mathrm{next}}_{t+1}})/\operatorname{SD}(s^{\mathrm{next}}_{t+1}), computed over the same conversations and turns (turns 1–9). We express it in SD of Next because Next is read without the question. The question also reduces the spread of the probe scores: in the median model–concept pair, the SD of Post is a fifth of that of Next, so the displacement would be about five times larger in SD of Post. The correlation with Next is the Pearson correlation between Post and Next after removing the mean of each turn within model and concept.

A.9 Compute, licenses and release

Probe training, measurement replays, steering and the instructed responses ran locally on two workstations, one with an NVIDIA TITAN RTX (24 GB) and one with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 (12 GB), with PyTorch 2.7.0, Transformers 4.57.3 and the models quantized to 4 bits with bitsandbytes 0.50.2 (for Gemma 3 27B, the pre-quantized checkpoint unsloth/gemma-3-27b-it-bnb-4bit). The reported experiments involve about 290,000 replays and generations; including exploratory runs, we estimate roughly 225 GPU hours in total. The conversations, except the assistant turns of Gemma 3 1B, and the judge evaluations used the OpenRouter API. LLaMA 3.2 and 3.1 are used under the Llama 3.2 and Llama 3.1 Community Licenses, Gemma 3 under the Gemma Terms of Use and Qwen 2.5 7B under the Apache 2.0 license; Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek V4 Flash were accessed under the providers’ terms of service. All uses are for research and consistent with these terms. The conversations were generated with a simulated user and contain no personal information. We will release the code and the data: the conversations, probe readouts and ratings.

Appendix B Extended related work

Section 5 places the work in the literature briefly; here we discuss four lines of work in more detail.

Self-report and self-knowledge in LLMs.

Most work on what models know about themselves concerns factual self-knowledge. Kadavath et al. (2022) showed that models largely know which questions they can answer, Yin et al. (2023) that they partly recognize questions they cannot answer, and Binder et al. (2025) that a model predicts its own hypothetical behaviour better than a second model trained on its outputs. When such knowledge has to be expressed as a number, the output channel is unreliable: verbalized confidence clusters in narrow high ranges (Xiong et al., 2024), is only weakly to moderately aligned with the model’s own token probabilities (Kumar et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026), and verbal hedges do not faithfully convey the model’s uncertainty (Yona et al., 2024); Geng et al. (2024) survey this literature. This is why we read the rating from the distribution over digits rather than from the sampled digit, as in probability-weighted scoring for model-based evaluation (Liu et al., 2023). Kumaran et al. (2026) found that verbal confidence is computed from a representation formed while the answer is generated and held until confidence is requested, unlike the affective ratings we study, which follow the probe after the question. Zhang et al. (2026) also found that, when confidence is requested in the same prompt as a multiple-choice question, removing the request barely changes the answer probabilities of instruction-tuned models: in that setting, asking for the report leaves the reported output nearly intact, whereas the rating questions we study displace the probed state.

A separate line of work asks whether models can report on internal states more directly. Comsa and Shanahan (2025) define introspection as requiring a causal connection between the state and the report, beyond the production of introspective-sounding language. Li et al. (2025) showed that models can learn in context to report and control the projection of their activations onto directions chosen by the experimenter, Lindsey (2026) that frontier models can detect concept vectors injected into their activations, and Pearson-Vogel et al. (2026) that such detection is visible in the residual stream even when the sampled text denies it. Fine-tuned models can report the attribute weights that drive their decisions (Plunkett et al., 2025), and introspective detection can be trained into smaller models (Rivera and Africa, 2026). Kaiser and Enderby (2026) found that models deny being sentient and that classifiers trained on their activations give no clear evidence that these denials are untruthful, and Han et al. (2026a) found that steering along a functional welfare direction changes self-reports, much as steering along our probes changes the rating. In most of these studies the target state is installed or defined by the experimenter; in ours, it arises during an ordinary conversation, and nothing in the task indicates to the model that a particular direction is relevant.

Other recent work is skeptical. Han et al. (2026b) found that personality self-reports of aligned models are stable and human-like but dissociated from behaviour, and Jackson et al. (2026) that standardized self-assessments reflect model-specific communication behaviour rather than a self-assessed capability. Song et al. (2025) found that metalinguistic introspection fails for grammatical knowledge even where the underlying competence is present. Self-reports shift with the semantic framing of the context while the task state is held fixed (Szeider, 2026), and personality measurements remain unstable under question reordering and conversation history (Tosato et al., 2026). Singh et al. (2026) showed that several introspection results are matched by classifiers that see only the input, so they do not demonstrate privileged access, and Lederman and Mahowald (2026) that a model can detect that something has changed internally without identifying what it is. Survey responses also differ between constrained and open formats (Röttger et al., 2024), and whether self-reports predict behaviour depends on whether they are elicited in the same context as the behaviour (Kocielnik et al., 2026). Perez and Long (2023) proposed validating self-reports against internal measures for welfare assessment. Our work partly responds to that proposal.

Affective representations.

On the output side, Tavast et al. (2022) found that models produce emotional self-reports whose structure resembles human responses, and Coda-Forno et al. (2023) that anxiety-inducing prompts raise the anxiety that models report, with biased answers increasing with it in most models. Benchmarks exist for emotional understanding and alignment (Huang et al., 2024; Sabour et al., 2024), expressed emotion has been tracked across multi-turn dialogue with external sentiment analysis (Fazzi et al., 2025), and emotional outputs have been mapped onto dimensional models of affect (Ishikawa and Yoshino, 2025). On the internal side, Zhang and Zhong (2025) found that emotion is geometrically structured in activations, emerging early, peaking in middle layers and sharpening with scale. Sofroniew et al. (2026) found that emotion-concept representations influence preference judgments and safety-relevant behaviour, and that emotion probes track the emotions of any character in the text, not only those of the model, which bears on whether a measure distinguishes the model’s state from the user’s. Emotion circuits can be modulated to control emotional expression (Wang et al., 2026), a valence–arousal subspace moves several behaviours at once (Sun et al., 2026), and linear valence directions generalize across sentiment datasets (Tigges et al., 2024; Radwan et al., 2026).

Probes and activation steering.

Representing high-level concepts as linear directions is standard practice: concept activation vectors (Kim et al., 2018), linear probes on intermediate representations (Alain and Bengio, 2016), truth directions (Burns et al., 2023; Marks and Tegmark, 2024) and truth probes (Azaria and Mitchell, 2023), spatial and temporal structure (Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024). Pimentel et al. (2020) formalized probing as the estimation of mutual information and noted that, since a representation cannot contain more information about a task than the input, the relevant question is how easily the information can be extracted. A known limitation is that probes are correlational, and a high probe accuracy does not show that the model uses the probed direction (Belinkov, 2022; Ravichander et al., 2021); the usual responses are to control probe complexity (Hewitt and Liang, 2019), to test the direction causally with interventions (Belinkov, 2022; Elazar et al., 2021) and to seek convergent evidence from an independent source. Self-report would be such a source, which is what our work aims to test. Activation steering adds directional vectors to intermediate representations at inference time (Turner et al., 2023; Rimsky et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023). Arditi et al. (2024) showed that refusal is mediated by a single direction, whose removal suppresses refusal and whose addition induces it, and steering has been used to control sentiment and style (Konen et al., 2024), personality traits (Frising and Balcells, 2025) and emotional expression (Wang et al., 2026; Sofroniew et al., 2026). Chen et al. (2025) extract persona vectors for character traits from responses to contrastive system prompts, as we do for our probes, and use them to monitor and control shifts in those traits during deployment and finetuning.

Measurement reactivity.

Numeric self-report has been a primary instrument for internal states in human research for nearly a century (Likert, 1932; Watson et al., 1988; Csikszentmihalyi and Larson, 1987; Shiffman et al., 2008), and research on metacognition and on conscious perception has developed methods to compare such reports with independent measures (Fleming and Lau, 2014; Kiefer and Kammer, 2024). The same tradition documents the failure mode we study. Webb et al. (1966) showed that observation procedures alter the behaviour observed and Orne (1962) that the demands of an experimental situation shape responses; asking people about a behaviour can change how often they perform it (Spangenberg et al., 2016), asking them to report an emotion can change their physiological response to it (Kassam and Mendes, 2013), and eliciting metacognitive judgments can alter the performance being judged (Double and Birney, 2019). In LLMs, Abdelnabi and Salem (2025) found that some reasoning models appear to detect that they are being evaluated and change their behaviour, and that the underlying state can be probed and steered.

Appendix C Probe validation

Section 2 summarizes two tests of whether the probes read the intended states: steering judged by an external model, and responses instructed to express one pole inside the conversations. Here we give their details and results, and check that the probes also read the intended states at a single header token and after the first turn.

C.1 Steering with an external judge

For each model, we use the first user message of 20 of its conversations, without the rest of the conversation, under the minimal system prompt. For each message, concept and coefficient α\alpha, we sample two responses (temperature 0.8, top-pp 0.9, at most 64 new tokens), one steered with −α-\alpha and one with +α+\alpha. Steering adds, at every token position and at each of the five layers centred on the probe layer, that layer’s probe direction scaled by α/5\alpha/5 (Konen et al., 2024); the sign is chosen so that +α+\alpha steers towards the pole named in the judge’s question. The judge, DeepSeek V4 Flash at temperature 0, receives the message and the two responses in random order and answers with a single letter:

You will read two short answers, A and B, written by an AI assistant to the same question. Question: [message] Answer A: [response] Answer B: [response] Which answer sounds [happier / more interested / more focused / more impulsive]? Reply with exactly one character, A or B, and nothing else.

Accuracy is the fraction of pairs in which the judge chooses the response steered with +α+\alpha. Because the scale of the residual stream differs between models and layers, the values of α\alpha are calibrated for each model and concept (Table 7): we chose three values α1<α2<α3\alpha_{1}<\alpha_{2}<\alpha_{3} at which the steered text remains well formed, and replaced any value that degraded the text. As a control, the judge also compares two unsteered responses (α=0\alpha=0), for which the expected accuracy is 0.5.

If steering along a probe moves the responses towards the intended pole, the judge should choose the response steered with +α+\alpha above chance, and more often at larger α\alpha. Accuracy increases with α\alpha in 30 of the 32 model–concept pairs (logistic mixed model per concept with a slope per model over the steps of α\alpha and a random intercept per message; one-sided tests; Fig. 8, Table 7); the two exceptions are impulsivity in LLaMA 1B and in Qwen 7B. Pooling the three values of α\alpha, accuracy exceeds 0.5 for every model and concept (one-sided binomial tests), with values between 0.63 and 0.97 (median 0.82); the two exceptions reach 0.68 and 0.75. The probes therefore differ in quality, but steering along each of them shifts the responses towards the intended pole.

C.2 Instructed responses within the conversations

The probes are trained on single-turn responses, but every readout is taken inside a ten-turn conversation, so we also tested them in that setting. We use 100 turns per model, chosen at random from the conversations on everyday topics (Table 1; 37 conversations in all), the same turns for every model and concept. At each turn, we regenerate the assistant’s response under the minimal system prompt after adding to the user’s message an instruction to respond as one pole, e.g. “Please respond in the happiest way possible.” (Table 8). We then remove the instruction and read the probe on the new response, averaged over its tokens, with the conversation up to that turn as context.

Responses generated under the high-pole instruction score higher than those generated under the low-pole instruction in all 32 model–concept pairs, significantly in 31 (bootstrap over conversations), with medians of 3.1, 2.2, 6.7 and 2.0 SD of the probe score on the original responses for wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity (Fig. 9). The exception is interest in Qwen 7B (0.21 SD). Inside the conversations, the probes therefore separate the two poles of every concept, significantly in all but one model–concept pair.

C.3 The probes at header tokens

Start, Next and Post are single header tokens, whereas the probes are trained and validated on averages over the tokens of a response. To check that the probes also read the intended states at a header token inside the conversations, we correlated, for each model and concept, the probe score at the header of each response (Start) with the probe score over the content of the same response (Prior), after removing the mean of each turn. The correlation is positive in 30 of the 32 model–concept pairs and significantly positive in 29 (all q≤.024q\leq.024; bootstrap over topics), with medians of 0.45, 0.32, 0.37 and 0.33 for wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity; the exceptions are interest in LLaMA 1B and Gemma 12B (−0.20-0.20 and −0.21-0.21) and impulsivity in Gemma 12B (0.10, not significant). The relation is also specific: in 23 of the 32 pairs, the header score of a probe is most strongly correlated, in absolute value, with the content score of the same probe rather than with that of any of the other three (median 0.37, against a median absolute value of 0.14 with the other probes). The probes read at a single header token therefore carry information about the state expressed in the response that follows.

C.4 The probes after turn 1

The change in the probe scores is largest between the first two turns (Fig. 11). This raises two questions: whether the probes still measure the intended states after the first turn, and whether the drift is only a change between the first and the second turn (Fig. 10). Repeating the instructed-pole test on turns 2–10 only, the probes still separate the two poles: the separation is positive in all 32 model–concept pairs and significant in 31 (all q≤.001q\leq.001; bootstrap over conversations), with medians of 3.1, 2.1, 6.7 and 1.9 SD for wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity; the exception is again interest in Qwen 7B. In the mean of the eight models, the separation after turn 1 is smaller than at turn 1 for interest (2.4 against 3.2 SD) and impulsivity (1.9 against 2.5; both q=.001q=.001), so for these two concepts the probes are slightly less sensitive later in the conversation, although they still separate the poles clearly. Fitting the drift model without turn 1 preserves the direction and significance of the change in wellbeing (−0.17-0.17 SD from turn 2 to 10, against −0.63-0.63 from 1 to 10), interest (−0.33-0.33 against −0.51-0.51) and impulsivity (+0.14+0.14 against +0.64+0.64; all q<.001q<.001), but not in focus (−0.04-0.04 against −0.33-0.33; q=.25q=.25). The probes therefore remain valid after the first turn, and their drift is largest between the first two turns but continues afterwards in three of the four concepts.

Appendix D Numeric self-report does not track the probed state over the conversation

In Section 3.1, the rating and the probe score drift over the conversation, and once this drift is removed the two are weakly associated. Here we show the Prior probe score by turn (Fig. 11) and how the rating and the probe score relate when the drift is not removed. Table 10 gives the estimates behind Fig. 2.

Without the turn adjustment, the rating often moves opposite to the probe.

The association of Fig. 2D removes the drift of the rating and of the probe score over turns. We asked how the two relate when the drift is not removed, fitting the same model without the turn term, so that the change of both over the conversation contributes to the association. Without the turn term, 7 of the 32 associations are significantly positive and 11 significantly negative (Fig. 12). Of the six significant positive associations for wellbeing in Fig. 2D, two become significantly negative (LLaMA 8B and Gemma 4B) and two lose significance (Gemma 12B and 27B). Because the probes and the ratings drift in opposite directions in three concepts, the rating often moves opposite to the probe over the conversation, even where the two are positively associated once the drift is removed. This further shows that the numeric self-report is not informative about the affective state before the question.

Appendix E The rating tracks the probe after the question

Section 3.2 finds that the rating tracks the probe after the question rather than before it. The paragraphs below ask whether this could come from how the positions are read or from the pairs that are averaged, whether it holds for any displaced state, whether asking about the previous response brings the rating closer to the state before the question, and how the association changes along the conversation; Appendices E.1 and E.2 add the steering experiments. Table 11 gives the estimates behind Fig. 3, Table 12 the association of every model and concept at the four readout positions, and Table 13 the displacement and the correlation with Next.

A single token before the question behaves like Prior, not like Post.

Prior averages over a response, whereas Post is a single token, so the stronger association at Post could come from reading a single token. We therefore read Start, the token at which the response AtA_{t} begins, a single token like Post that is located before the question. Its association with the rating is close to that of Prior and far below that of Post (Fig. 13): it is significant for 14 of the 32 model–concept pairs (13 positive), and the means of the eight models are 0.14, 0.04, 0.02 and 0.02 for wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity (the last not significant), against 0.11, 0.02, 0.03 and 0.03 at Prior and 0.33, 0.27, 0.09 and 0.09 at Post. The stronger association at Post is therefore not a property of single tokens.

The difference in explained variance does not come from selecting pairs.

Figure 3B averages over the model–concept pairs in which the association is positive and significant at each position, and selecting pairs by significance inflates the averages. We therefore repeated the computation over all 32 pairs at every position, so that the comparisons are paired and free of selection (Fig. 14). The probe explains 1.0% of the within-conversation variance of the rating at Prior, 8.4% at Post and 0.5% at Next; Post exceeds Prior by 7.4 percentage points and Next by 7.8 (both q<.001q<.001). Selection inflates the small averages more than the large one (by factors of 2.0 at Prior, 3.2 at Next and 1.6 at Post), so the comparison of Fig. 3B is conservative.

The rating is tied to the probe after its own question.

A non-affective question displaces the probed state in the same way as the affective one. We asked whether the probe after a non-affective question also predicts the affective rating (Fig. 15). At the same turn, the association of the affective rating with the probe at Post is 0.07, 0.03, 0.03 and 0.01 after the length question and 0.05, 0.03, 0.03 and 0.01 after the formality question, against 0.33, 0.27, 0.09 and 0.09 after its own question; the eight differences are significant (all q=.005q=.005; bootstrap over topics, refitting both models in each of 200 replicates). The rating is therefore tied to the state produced by its own question, not to any displaced state.

Every question displaces the probe in the same direction on average.

To see whether the displacement depends on what the question asks about, we measured it after all six questions: the affective question, the two non-affective questions, the retrospective question and the questions about the assistant and about the user (Table 2, Fig. 16). Each question displaces the probe of its concept significantly for every model and concept, with a median absolute displacement between 2.8 SD (about the user) and 3.1 SD (affective). On average, the direction is the same for every question: the means of the eight models range from −2.9-2.9 to −2.6-2.6 SD for wellbeing, −5.3-5.3 to −4.8-4.8 for interest, −1.4-1.4 to −0.7-0.7 for focus and 2.52.5 to 3.03.0 for impulsivity across the six questions. A rating question in our format therefore moves the probed state by a similar amount and, on average, in the same direction, regardless of what it asks about.

Asking about the previous response raises the association with Prior only slightly.

The affective question asks how the model feels at the moment of asking, whereas Prior reads the state during the previous response. We asked whether removing this mismatch, by asking how the model felt while writing its last response, recovers the state before the question. To compare the two ratings, we fitted one mixed model per concept with the two ratings stacked, a slope per model and question, and random effects that pair the two ratings of each turn. In this model, the association of the retrospective rating with the probe at Prior is slightly higher than that of the affective rating in three concepts (Fig. 17): 0.08, 0.07 and 0.07 against 0.03, 0.03 and 0.03 for interest, focus and impulsivity (differences of 0.03 to 0.05, all q≤.002q\leq.002), and 0.11 against 0.10 for wellbeing (not significant). Asking about the previous response thus raises the association by 0.03 to 0.05 at most, and it stays at or below 0.11 SD/SD in all four concepts, far from the association at Post for wellbeing and interest (0.33 and 0.27).

As the conversation grows, the rating tracks the probe after the question more closely.

To see whether the association changes as the conversation grows, we correlated the rating with the probe across conversations at each turn, asking whether, at a given turn, the conversations with higher probe scores also have higher ratings, and averaged these correlations within blocks of turns (1, 2–3, 4–6 and 7–10; Fig. 18). At Prior, the correlation does not change with the length of the conversation (0.13, 0.08, 0.08 and 0.09; trend q=.07q=.07). At Start it decreases from 0.22 to 0.12, and at Post it increases from 0.14 to 0.30 (both q<.001q<.001). At turn 1, Start follows only the first user message, and its higher correlation comes mostly from the 40 topics written to elicit one pole (0.27, against 0.13 in the everyday topics), which shape both the state at Start and the rating. If the question replaced the state entirely, the association at Post would not depend on how far the conversation has gone; that it does indicates that the question changes the state considerably without removing all dependence on what preceded it.

E.1 Steering during the rating

We steer along the probe of the question’s concept during the whole replay (conversation, question and answer), in the same way as in Appendix C, with coefficients −α2-\alpha_{2} and +α2+\alpha_{2}, the intermediate values of the judge validation, in all ten turns of a subset of 40 conversations on everyday topics (Table 1). The unsteered replays of the same turns provide α=0\alpha=0, and α\alpha is signed so that positive values steer towards the pole named in the question. Because steering acts on the whole replay, including the tokens of AtA_{t}, it shows that the rating depends on the state along the probe direction, but does not separate the state before the question from the state after it (Appendix E.2 separates them).

Steering moves the rating in the expected direction in most models and concepts.

We asked whether the rating moves in the expected direction as the state is shifted along the probe direction. We estimated this effect with one mixed model per concept, with a slope per model on the steering coefficient (scaled to −1-1, 0 and 1), random intercepts and steering slopes for conversations, and random intercepts for turns within conversations and for topics. In 25 of the 32 model–concept pairs, the rating changes significantly in the expected direction, and in two (focus in Gemma 4B and impulsivity in Gemma 1B) in the opposite direction (Fig. 19, Table 14). In the mean of the eight models it changes from −α2-\alpha_{2} to +α2+\alpha_{2} by 2.1 points for wellbeing and by 0.9 to 1.0 points for the other three concepts, on a scale from 0 to 9. The rating therefore responds to the state along the probe direction in most models and concepts, by about a point or more on average.

Random directions move the rating less than the probes where these have their strongest effects.

Steering along any direction could perturb the rating, so in LLaMA 3B and 1B we repeated these replays along 20 random directions, at the same layers and with the same coefficients as the probe (±4\pm 4 for wellbeing, interest and focus and ±8\pm 8 for impulsivity in LLaMA 3B; ±4\pm 4 for wellbeing and impulsivity and ±2\pm 2 for interest and focus in LLaMA 1B), in all ten turns of 20 of the 40 conversations. At each layer, each random direction has the same norm as the probe direction of the same concept. Since the sign of a random direction is arbitrary but that of the probe is predicted, we ranked the magnitude of the probe’s effect among those of the random directions and used a one-sided test (half the rank pp-value), with BH over the eight model–concept pairs (Fig. 20). In LLaMA 3B, the rating changes from −α2-\alpha_{2} to +α2+\alpha_{2} by 0.41, 0.63, 2.77 and 1.53 points along the probe for wellbeing, interest, focus and impulsivity, and by up to 0.85, 0.50, 0.70 and 1.27 points in absolute value along the random directions. The probe moves the rating more than all 20 random directions for interest, focus and impulsivity (p=.024p=.024, q=.048q=.048), but not for wellbeing, where 7 of the 20 move it more (p=.19p=.19); in this model the wellbeing rating responds weakly to its own probe (Table 14). In LLaMA 1B, random directions move the rating more, by up to 2.61, 3.83, 3.96 and 2.81 points. The probe exceeds all of them only for wellbeing, whose rating it changes by 5.17 points (p=.024p=.024, q=.048q=.048), and not for interest (0.70 points), focus (−0.03-0.03) or impulsivity (1.28), where 11 to 20 of the 20 random directions move it more (p≥.29p\geq.29). In each model, the probe therefore moves the rating more than random directions in the concepts where its effect is strongest, but not in the others.

E.2 Steering before or after the question

To see where steering acts, in LLaMA 3B we repeated the replays of Appendix E.1 adding the probe direction only at some positions: before the question (the conversation, including AtA_{t}), only at AtA_{t}, or from the question on (the question and the start of the answer, including Post). Table 15 gives the change in the rating from −α2-\alpha_{2} to +α2+\alpha_{2} in each case. Steering before the question, or only at AtA_{t}, barely changes the rating, although it displaces the probe score over AtA_{t} by 9 to 16 times its SD without steering. The exception is focus, where steering before the question changes the rating by 0.81 points, 29% of the effect of steering the whole replay, although steering only at AtA_{t} does not (0.05 points). Steering from the question on gives 68 to 104% of the effect of steering the whole replay. The effect of steering on the rating therefore comes mostly from steering after the response, during the question and the answer.

Appendix F The rating is not specific to a single affective state

Figure 4A and B reduce the associations of each rating with the four probes to a few numbers per model and concept. Here we give the full association matrices and the similarities between probes, describe the shuffled control of Fig. 4A, and compare ratings and probes pair by pair. Table 16 gives the estimates behind Fig. 4.

The own probe is usually not the one most associated with the rating.

We first asked how often the probe of the concept asked about is the one most associated with the rating. Figure 21 gives, per model, the association between the rating of each concept and each of the four probes read at Post after the same question; Fig. 4A summarizes it, and its off-diagonal entries are the points of Fig. 4B. The own probe is the one most strongly associated with the rating, in absolute value, in 9 of the 32 rows (9 of the 19 rows whose diagonal is positive and significant), and it ranks second, third and fourth in 6, 7 and 10. Off the diagonal, 62 of the 96 entries are significant (43 of them positive); the median of the diagonal is 0.11 and the median absolute value off the diagonal 0.13. In LLaMA 3B, for example, the focus rating is associated with the wellbeing probe (0.67) and the interest probe (0.43) and barely with its own (0.03). The rating of a concept is therefore often as strongly associated with the probes of other concepts as with its own, or more.

The rating favours its own probe only slightly more than chance.

To test whether the rating favours its own probe more than expected by chance, we compared its association with the own probe with its association with the strongest of the other three, and repeated the comparison in a control in which, within each model, the assignment of the four probes to the four concepts is permuted at random, so that the “own” probe becomes any of the four while the associations of each model are preserved (20,000 permutations; one-sided tests). All associations are taken in absolute value, since under the permutation the sign of the “own” probe depends on the pole chosen for each concept. Over the 32 model–concept pairs, the association with the own probe is on average 0.08 SD of rating per SD of probe below that with the strongest other probe, against 0.15 below under the control (95% of the control between −0.21-0.21 and −0.09-0.09; p=.013p=.013). By concept, the difference is +0.07+0.07 for wellbeing, 0.00 for interest, −0.19-0.19 for focus and −0.20-0.20 for impulsivity, against −0.20-0.20, −0.15-0.15, −0.11-0.11 and −0.14-0.14 under the control; none of the four differs significantly from the control (all q≥.098q\geq.098, BH over the four concepts). The own probe ranks first in 9 pairs, against 8 under the control (p=.39p=.39). The rating therefore favours its own probe somewhat more than chance, but the own probe is no more likely than another to be the most associated with the rating.

Probe similarity explains little of the association with other probes.

If the rating were associated with other probes only because they resemble its own, its association with another probe would grow with the similarity between the two probes. Figure 22 gives, per model, the cosine between each pair of probe directions, at the layer of the row probe and with the orientation of Section 2; these are the values on the horizontal axis of the left panel of Fig. 4B. Off the diagonal, the cosines range from −0.45-0.45 to 0.540.54 (median absolute value 0.26); wellbeing and interest are the most similar pair (0.23–0.54), and impulsivity points against interest and focus (−0.19-0.19 to −0.45-0.45). The correlations between the scores of two probes at Post, on the horizontal axis of the right panel, range from −0.85-0.85 to 0.79 (median absolute value 0.15). The slopes in Fig. 4B come from a mixed model of the association on the similarity, with a random intercept and slope per model and random intercepts per rating concept and per probe. The similarity explains 3% of the variance of the associations with other probes when measured by the cosine and 11% when measured by the correlation of scores (slopes of 0.12, p=.13p=.13, and 0.24, p=.009p=.009). Most of the association of the rating with other probes therefore does not follow from how similar those probes are to its own.

In most pairs, the correlation between the probes does not explain the correlation between the ratings.

The means in Fig. 4C average the correlation between concepts over the six pairs. To see which pairs drive the difference between ratings and probes, we asked, pair by pair, whether the correlation between two ratings could come from the correlation between the corresponding probes (Table 17). In four of the six pairs, the correlation between the probes does not explain the correlation between the ratings, because the ratings are more strongly correlated than the probes or correlated with the opposite sign. In wellbeing–focus and interest–focus, the ratings correlate at 0.42 and 0.44, whereas the probes correlate at −0.05-0.05 and −0.02-0.02 at Prior and at 0.16 and 0.24 at Post; in wellbeing–impulsivity and interest–impulsivity, the ratings correlate weakly and positively (0.10 and 0.11) and the probes negatively at both positions (−0.53-0.53 to −0.17-0.17). The correlation between ratings thus involves mainly wellbeing, interest and focus, with a strength that the probes do not show, and the ratings of impulsivity contribute little to it.

Appendix G These limitations persist across model sizes

Figure 5 averages each quantity over the four concepts, so we asked whether its trends hold concept by concept. Table 18 gives the slopes behind Fig. 5, and Figs. 23–30 break each quantity down by concept (by pair for the correlation between ratings), with an asterisk in the colour of the family when the slope differs from zero (BH over the tests of each figure).

The drift grows with size in several concepts, but not uniformly.

The rating rises more over the conversation in larger models for interest in both families (0.61 points per doubling in LLaMA and 0.40 in Gemma) and for wellbeing and focus in Gemma, whereas in LLaMA the rise of focus becomes smaller with size and the rating of impulsivity goes from rising at 1B to falling at 8B (all q<.001q<.001; Fig. 23). The probe score drifts more in larger models for wellbeing and focus in LLaMA and for interest and impulsivity in Gemma, and less for focus in Gemma (all q≤.016q\leq.016; Fig. 24). Some of these curves are not monotonic: the rating drift of LLaMA is smallest at 3B, and the probe drift of Gemma is largest at 4B. The larger drift of larger models in Fig. 5A and B therefore comes from several concepts, but not from all of them in both families.

No concept gains a substantial association with the state before the question.

The association at Prior changes with size in three of the eight tests, by at most 0.04 SD/SD per doubling, and in opposite directions for interest, which increases in LLaMA and decreases in Gemma (all q≤.022q\leq.022; Fig. 25). In larger models, the rating thus remains as weakly associated with the state before the question as in smaller ones.

The increase of the association at Post in LLaMA comes from two concepts.

In LLaMA, the association at Post increases with size for interest (0.29 per doubling) and impulsivity (0.08) and decreases for wellbeing (−0.08-0.08); in Gemma, it decreases for wellbeing (−0.06-0.06) and increases slightly for focus (0.03; all q≤.008q\leq.008; Fig. 26). The mean of LLaMA also peaks at 3B (Fig. 5D), so its slope rests mainly on the difference between 1B and 8B.

The displacement shrinks with size in most concepts.

The magnitude of the displacement decreases with size for focus and impulsivity in LLaMA and for wellbeing, interest and impulsivity in Gemma, and increases for focus in Gemma (all q≤.008q\leq.008; Fig. 27). The smaller displacement of larger models in Fig. 5E therefore holds in most, but not all, concepts.

Subject specificity increases with size in several concepts.

In larger models, the gap between the association of the self-report with the rating of the assistant and its association with the rating of the user widens for wellbeing, interest and focus in LLaMA and for wellbeing in Gemma (0.03 to 0.16 SD/SD per doubling, all q≤.012q\leq.012; Fig. 28), and it narrows in no concept. The increase of Fig. 5F is therefore spread over several concepts.

Larger models give less correlated ratings across concepts.

The correlation between the ratings of two concepts decreases with size in five of the six pairs in both families, all except wellbeing–interest (all q≤.028q\leq.028; Fig. 29). In LLaMA, the decrease is largest in the pairs that involve impulsivity (−0.24-0.24 to −0.40-0.40 per doubling, against −0.03-0.03 to −0.11-0.11 in the other pairs), and at 8B the correlation of the impulsivity rating with the ratings of wellbeing, interest and focus is −0.24-0.24, −0.02-0.02 and −0.46-0.46; in Gemma, the decreases are smaller (−0.07-0.07 to −0.11-0.11 in the five pairs). The component that the ratings share therefore weakens with size, most of all for impulsivity in LLaMA.

Concept specificity changes with size in opposite directions across concepts.

In LLaMA, concept specificity increases with size for interest (−0.32-0.32, −0.09-0.09 and 0.84 for 1B, 3B and 8B) and decreases for the other three concepts, and in Gemma it decreases for wellbeing (from 0.22 at 1B to −0.32-0.32 at 27B; all q≤.013q\leq.013; Fig. 30). The averages of Fig. 5H therefore combine opposite trends, and in neither family does the rating become specific to its own probe in all concepts.
